moduleMetadata.title: Data Handling & Privacy at Work
moduleMetadata.description: Understand how to identify, classify, and securely handle sensitive organizational and personal information.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Information is one of the most valuable assets in an organization. Everyday work involves customer information, student records, financial files, internal communications, passwords, and contracts. A security incident does not always require malware or hacking. Accidentally sending the right information to the wrong person can also become a serious security and privacy incident.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should understand how improper handling of data can create cybersecurity and privacy risks.

learningObjectives: Define sensitive information and personal data.
Apply data classification concepts (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted).
Practice safe data sharing and cloud storage awareness.
Recognize the risks of unauthorized disclosure and data leakage.
Understand the importance of privacy and correct recipient verification.

sections.title: What is Sensitive Information?
sections.content: Sensitive information is data that must be protected from unauthorized access to safeguard the privacy or security of an individual or organization.

subsections.title: Personal Data (PII)
subsections.content: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is any data that can be used to identify a specific person, such as name, social security number, or medical records.

subsections.title: Confidential Business Information
subsections.content: This includes trade secrets, financial records, and internal strategy documents.

sections.title: Data Classification
sections.content: Organizations often use levels to determine how data should be handled.

levels.label: Public
levels.description: Safe for everyone to see (e.g., marketing brochures).

levels.label: Internal
levels.description: Intended for employees only (e.g., company policies).

levels.label: Confidential
levels.description: Sensitive data requiring limited access (e.g., department budgets).

levels.label: Restricted/Secret
levels.description: Highly sensitive data (e.g., customer passwords, medical data).

sections.title: Safe Data Sharing
sections.content: How you share data is as important as what you share.
bulletPoints: Use encrypted links instead of attachments for sensitive files.
Set expiration dates on shared links.
Verify if the recipient is authorized to see the data.

sections.title: Cloud Storage and Privacy
sections.content: Cloud tools (like OneDrive, Google Drive, or Dropbox) are convenient but require careful permission management.
sections.tip: Avoid setting folders to 'Anyone with the link can view' unless the data is truly public.

interactiveExercises.title: Choose the Correct Data Classification
interactiveExercises.question: Match the following items to their correct classification level:

interactiveExercises.title: Wrong Recipient Simulation
interactiveExercises.question: You are about to send a spreadsheet with student grades. You type 'Accounting' and the auto-complete suggests 'accounting@example.net' (external) and 'accounting@your-org.edu' (internal). Which do you choose?
interactiveExercises.explanation: Always verify that the recipient's domain matches your organization for internal sensitive data.

scenarios.title: The Accounting Error
scenarios.content: You need to send a spreadsheet to 'accounts@example.com' but accidentally send it to 'accounting@example.net' because of auto-complete.
scenarios.lesson: Auto-complete is helpful but dangerous for sensitive data.

scenarios.title: The 'Reply All' Trap
scenarios.content: A colleague sends an email to 50 people. You reply with a confidential attachment meant only for the colleague, but you hit 'Reply All'.
scenarios.action: Immediately contact IT and the recipients to request deletion, and report the incident.
scenarios.lesson: Always check the 'To' and 'CC' fields before hitting send.

scenarios.title: Open Folder Risk
scenarios.content: You find a folder of salary information on the company cloud drive set to 'Anyone with the link can view'.
scenarios.action: Report it to the folder owner or IT immediately to restrict access.
scenarios.lesson: Permissions should always follow the 'Principle of Least Privilege'.

scenarios.title: The Curious Friend
scenarios.content: A friend in a different department asks to see a customer's record 'just to check something out' because they know you have access.
scenarios.action: Politely refuse. Access to data should only be for authorized business purposes.
scenarios.lesson: Unauthorized access, even by trusted colleagues, is a security violation.

quiz.question: What does PII stand for?
quiz.explanation: PII is data that can be used on its own or with other information to identify, contact, or locate a single person.

quiz.question: Which data classification level is appropriate for a company's public press release?
quiz.explanation: Public data is intended for general consumption.

quiz.question: The 'Principle of Least Privilege' means:
options: Giving everyone access to everything to be fair.
Giving users only the access they need to perform their job.
Only managers get to use the printer.
quiz.correctAnswer: Giving users only the access they need to perform their job.
quiz.explanation: This limits the potential damage from a compromised account or accidental error.

quiz.question: What is the danger of using 'Anyone with the link' for sensitive cloud files?
options: The link might expire too soon.
Anyone who finds or is forwarded the link can see the data without logging in.
It makes the files too large.
quiz.correctAnswer: Anyone who finds or is forwarded the link can see the data without logging in.
quiz.explanation: This bypasses identity verification and makes the data public.

quiz.question: Is it okay to store sensitive work data on a personal USB drive?
options: Yes, if you are working from home.
No, unless it is specifically authorized and the drive is encrypted.
Yes, as long as you don't lose it.
quiz.correctAnswer: No, unless it is specifically authorized and the drive is encrypted.
quiz.explanation: Unencrypted personal drives are a major source of data leakage.

quiz.question: What should you do if you receive an email with sensitive data that wasn't meant for you?
options: Read it and then delete it.
Notify the sender and delete the email.
quiz.correctAnswer: Notify the sender and delete the email.
quiz.explanation: This helps the sender correct their mistake and prevents further unauthorized access.

quiz.question: Data Leakage occurs when:
options: Sensitive data is transferred to an unauthorized person or destination.
quiz.correctAnswer: Sensitive data is transferred to an unauthorized person or destination.
quiz.explanation: Leakage can be accidental or intentional.

quiz.question: Which of these is a PII?
quiz.explanation: An ID number is a unique identifier linked to a specific person.

keyTakeaways: Identify the sensitivity of data before you handle it.
Verify recipients and permissions every single time.
Follow the Principle of Least Privilege.
reflectApply: Look at your recent outgoing emails. Did any contain sensitive data? Were the recipients correct?
Check the sharing settings on your most active cloud folder. Is access restricted to only those who need it?
